lead: Isaiah sings of a strong city whose walls are God's own saving work, and he gives the reason it stands: “in the Lord God you have an everlasting rock.” Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with two houses in one storm, and the rock now has a practical meaning: hearing his words and doing them. Advent is a good time to look at the foundations.

set: This song belongs to the same section as yesterday's feast (Isaiah 24–27). Two cities stand side by side there: the proud city that falls and the city of those who trust. Ancient people felt safe behind high walls. The song turns this upside down: the height falls, and the poor walk over it.
str: vv. 1–2: the strong city and its open gates.
vv. 3–4: trust in the Lord, the rock.
vv. 5–6: the lofty city laid low; the poor walk on it.
kw: A city with strength, but its walls here are God's “victory” or salvation (v. 1). Its security does not come from stone.
To lean on someone and feel safe. The word appears in both v. 3 and v. 4: trust is the only foundation the poet recommends.
Ṣûr is a great mass of rock, the mountain refuge of the land. Moses calls God “the Rock” in his song (Deuteronomy 32:4).
vv: Open the gates, so that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in.
The gates are open, not shut. What qualifies a person to enter is faithfulness, not birth or strength. Psalm 118, today's psalm, sings the same: “Open to me the gates of righteousness” (118:19).
Trust in the Lord forever, for in the Lord God you have an everlasting rock.
This is the centre of the reading and the bridge to the Gospel.
The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy.
God reverses the order of things, as Mary will sing: “He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly” (Luke 1:52).
ch: The Fathers and the liturgy read the rock as Christ, following St Paul: “the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The Lectionary puts this song beside the Gospel of the two houses for that reason. Advent asks whether our security rests on walls of our own or on him.

set: These are the closing words of the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7). The reading leaves out vv. 22–23, on those who did great things in Jesus' name and yet never knew him. In the land of Israel a dry valley can turn in an hour into a violent stream after the winter rain. Everyone listening would know how the house on the sand ends.
str: v. 21: not saying, but doing the Father's will.
vv. 24–25: the wise builder: same storm, house stands.
vv. 26–27: the foolish builder: same storm, great fall.
kw: A correct confession and a solemn title. But Jesus says it is not enough to say the right words.
Sensible, practical, knowing what the moment needs. The same word describes the wise bridesmaids (25:2). Its opposite is mōros, foolish.
The house “had been founded on rock” (v. 25). What matters happens before the storm, in the digging that no one sees.
vv: Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.
Jesus speaks here with an astonishing authority: he himself is the “Lord” of the last day. And he points beyond himself to “my Father”.
Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.
“These words of mine” take the place that the words of the Law hold in Israel's life. St James says the same: “be doers of the word, and not merely hearers” (James 1:22).
The rain fell, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on rock.
The rain falls on both houses. Faith is not a promise of no storms. The difference appears only when the weather comes.
ch: The Catechism teaches from v. 21 that prayer means disposing the heart to do the Father's will (CCC 2611), and that one enters the Kingdom not by speaking words but by doing that will (CCC 2826). St Augustine closes his commentary on the Sermon on the Mount with these two houses: to hear and not to do is to build without a foundation (in substance).

qa: Does this Gospel mean that we are saved by works and not by faith?

No. Jesus does not set faith against action; he sets empty words against a real life. St Paul speaks of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). Grace comes first and is a gift, and it builds the house; the doing is what faith looks like when it is alive.
rite: St Francis Xavier (1506–1552) was one of the first companions of St Ignatius of Loyola. He landed in Goa in 1542 and preached among the fishing people of the Fishery Coast and in Travancore, before going on to Malacca, the Moluccas and Japan. He died on the island of Shangchuan, off the coast of China, and his body lies in the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa. The Church honours him, with St Thérèse of Lisieux, as patron of the missions. He is a witness of today's Gospel for the Latin Catholics of India: a man who heard the words and acted on them.
study: If a storm came tomorrow, what in my life would stand? What would I find is built on sand?
St Francis Xavier gave up a promising career at the University of Paris to go to the ends of the known world. What word of Christ am I hearing without yet acting on it?
